The resulting positive charge on nitrogen strongly deactivates the benzene ring toward electrophilic substitution. Hence, aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation. Thus, Statement I is true.
Statement II: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis involves nucleophilic substitution (\(\text{S}_{\text{N}}2\)) of potassium phthalimide anion on an alkyl halide. Aryl halides (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{X}\)) do not undergo nucleophilic substitution under mild conditions due to partial double-bond character of the \(\text{C--X}\) bond. Consequently, aromatic primary amines like aniline cannot be prepared by Gabriel synthesis. Thus, Statement II is true.

Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

answer.text: Statement I is correct but Statement II is false.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q70 - Highest number of helium atoms in given quantities

questiontext.text: The highest number of helium atoms is in

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
1. \(4\ \text{g}\) of helium
2. \(2.271098\ \text{L}\) of helium at STP
3. \(4\ \text{mol}\) of helium
4. \(4\ \text{u}\) of helium
Molar mass of helium: \(M = 4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard mole concept definitions apply (\(1\ \text{mol} = N_{\text{A}} \approx 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms).

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of atoms \(N = n \times N_{\text{A}}\), where \(n\) is the amount in moles.

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For \(4\ \text{g}\) of helium:
\[ n = \frac{4\ \text{g}}{4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 1\ \text{mol} \implies N_1 = 1 N_{\text{A}} \text{ atoms} \]
2. For \(2.271098\ \text{L}\) of helium at STP (molar volume \(= 22.71\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\)):
\[ n = \frac{2.271098}{22.71} \approx 0.1\ \text{mol} \implies N_2 = 0.1 N_{\text{A}} \text{ atoms} \]
3. For \(4\ \text{mol}\) of helium:
\[ n = 4\ \text{mol} \implies N_3 = 4 N_{\text{A}} \text{ atoms} \]
4. For \(4\ \text{u}\) of helium:
\[ N_4 = 1 \text{ atom} \]

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The maximum number of helium atoms is in \(4\ \text{mol}\) of helium (\(4 N_{\text{A}}\) atoms).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q71 - Organic reactions and corresponding reagents

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II.

List I (Reaction) with List II (Reagents/Condition):

A. \(\text{R-CH}=\text{CH}_2 \to \text{R-CHO}\)
B. Benzene \(\to\) Benzophenone
C. Cyclohexanol \(\to\) Cyclohexanone
D. \(\text{R-CH}_2-\text{CH}_3 \to \text{R-COOH}\)

I. \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} / \text{anhydrous } \text{AlCl}_3\)
II. \(\text{CrO}_3\)
III. \(\text{KMnO}_4 / \text{KOH}, \Delta\)
IV. (i) \(\text{O}_3\), (ii) \(\text{Zn-H}_2\text{O}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Organic functional group transformations require specific oxidizing agents or electrophilic substitution reagents.

Evaluation of Matches
A. Reductive ozonolysis of terminal alkenes (\(\text{R-CH}=\text{CH}_2\)) using (i) \(\text{O}_3\) and (ii) \(\text{Zn-H}_2\text{O}\) yields aldehydes (\(\text{R-CHO}\)) (Match IV).
B. Conversion of benzene to benzophenone is a Friedel-Crafts acylation using benzoyl chloride (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}\)) in the presence of anhydrous \(\text{AlCl}_3\) (Match I).
C. Oxidation of secondary alcohols (cyclohexanol) to ketones (cyclohexanone) is carried out using chromic anhydride (\(\text{CrO}_3\)) (Match II).
D. Vigorous oxidation of alkyl side chains on aromatic/aliphatic systems to carboxylic acids is achieved using alkaline \(\text{KMnO}_4/\text{KOH}\) with heating (\(\Delta\)) (Match III).

Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q72 - Reagents for alkene to aldehyde transformation

questiontext.text: Identify the correct reagents that would bring about the following transformation.

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Converting a terminal alkene to an aldehyde with the same carbon count requires anti-Markovnikov hydration to a primary alcohol followed by selective mild oxidation to an aldehyde.

Evaluation
1. Hydroboration-oxidation using (i) \(\text{BH}_3\) followed by (ii) alkaline \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^-\) adds water across the double bond in an anti-Markovnikov fashion, converting the terminal alkene into a primary alcohol (\(\text{R-CH}_2\text{--}\text{CH}_2\text{--}\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)).
2. Controlled oxidation of the primary alcohol using Pyridinium Chlorochromate ((iii) \(\text{PCC}\)) yields the corresponding aldehyde (\(\text{R-CH}_2\text{--}\text{CH}_2\text{--}\text{CHO}\)) without over-oxidizing it to a carboxylic acid.

Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of reagents is (i) \(\text{BH}_3\), (ii) \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^-\), (iii) \(\text{PCC}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q73 - Fastest rate of SN1 reaction in organobromides

questiontext.text: The compound that will undergo \(\text{S}_{\text{N}}1\) reaction with the fastest rate is

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The rate of an \(\text{S}_{\text{N}}1\) reaction is governed by the rate-determining step involving heterolytic cleavage of the \(\text{C--X}\) bond to form a carbocation intermediate. The reaction rate is directly proportional to carbocation stability.

Evaluation
- Bromobenzene does not undergo \(\text{S}_{\text{N}}1\) due to partial double bond character and extreme instability of the phenyl cation.
- Primary and secondary aliphatic alkyl bromides form secondary or primary carbocations stabilized only by inductive and hyperconjugative effects.
- 1-Phenylethyl bromide (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{--}\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{--}\text{CH}_3\)) forms a secondary benzylic carbocation (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{--}\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}\text{--}\text{CH}_3\)), which is extraordinarily stabilized by resonance delocalization of positive charge into the aromatic \(\pi\)-system as well as hyperconjugation from the methyl group.

Final Conclusion
1-Phenylethyl bromide undergoes \(\text{S}_{\text{N}}1\) reaction at the fastest rate.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q74 - Composition of Fehling solution A

questiontext.text: Fehling's solution 'A' is

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Fehling's reagent is prepared by mixing two separate solutions, designated as Fehling's solution A and Fehling's solution B, in equal volumes immediately prior to testing.

Evaluation
- Fehling's solution A consists of an aqueous solution of copper sulphate (\(\text{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O}\)).
- Fehling's solution B consists of an alkaline solution of sodium potassium tartrate (Rochelle's salt).

Final Conclusion
Fehling's solution 'A' is aqueous copper sulphate.

answer.text: alkaline solution of sodium potassium tartrate (Rochelle's salt)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q75 - Most stable carbocation among aliphatic and cyclic ions

questiontext.text: The most stable carbocation among the following is:

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
List of candidate carbocations including primary, secondary, and tertiary structures.

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Relative stability of carbocations increases with degree of alkyl substitution (\(3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ}\)) due to hyperconjugation and inductive effects.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Each \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom attached to adjacent sp3-hybridized carbon atoms contributes to hyperconjugative stabilization of the positively charged carbon center.

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Identify the degree of substitution for each structure:
- Primary carbocation (\(1^{\circ}\)): least stable.
- Secondary carbocation (\(2^{\circ}\)): moderately stable.
- Tertiary carbocation (\(3^{\circ}\)): highly substituted with the maximum number of \(\alpha\)-hydrogens.
2. The tertiary (\(3^{\circ}\)) carbocation contains 3 attached alkyl groups, providing maximum hyperconjugative structures and strong \(+I\) inductive charge dispersal, making it significantly more stable than secondary or primary carbocations.

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The tertiary (\(3^{\circ}\)) carbocation is the most stable carbocation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q76 - Direction of chemical equilibrium from reaction quotient

questiontext.text:
For the reaction \(2\mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{B} + \mathrm{C}\), \(\mathrm{K_c} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\). At a given time, the composition of reaction mixture is: \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}] = [\mathrm{C}] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}\).

Then, which of the following is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reversible reaction: \(2\text{A} \rightleftharpoons \text{B} + \text{C}\)
Equilibrium constant: \(K_{\text{c}} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\)
Current concentrations: \([\text{A}] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}\), \([\text{B}] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}\), \([\text{C}] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}\)

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The reaction quotient \(Q_{\text{c}}\) indicates direction relative to equilibrium: if \(Q_{\text{c}} > K_{\text{c}}\), the reaction shifts backward.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Expression for the reaction quotient:
\[ Q_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\text{B}][\text{C}]}{[\text{A}]^2} \]

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute current concentrations into \(Q_{\text{c}}\):
\[ Q_{\text{c}} = \frac{(2 \times 10^{-3}) \times (2 \times 10^{-3})}{(2 \times 10^{-3})^2} = 1 \]
Compare \(Q_{\text{c}}\) with \(K_{\text{c}}\):
\[ Q_{\text{c}} = 1, \quad K_{\text{c}} = 0.004 \implies Q_{\text{c}} > K_{\text{c}} \]
Since \(Q_{\text{c}} > K_{\text{c}}\), the reaction contains an excess of products relative to equilibrium conditions.

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The reaction has a tendency to proceed in the backward direction to establish equilibrium.

answer.text: Reaction has a tendency to go in backward direction.
Reaction has gone to completion in forward direction.
Reaction has a tendency to go in forward direction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q77 - Gas solubility order from Henry law constants

questiontext.text: The Henry's law constant (\(\mathrm{K_H}\)) values of three gases (A, B, C) in water are \(145, 2 \times 10^{-5}\) and 35 kbar, respectively. The solubility of these gases in water follow the order:

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
Henry's law constant values:
\(K_{\text{H}}(\text{A}) = 145\ \text{kbar}\)
\(K_{\text{H}}(\text{B}) = 2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kbar}\)
\(K_{\text{H}}(\text{C}) = 35\ \text{kbar}\)

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All gases are compared at the same partial pressure and temperature in water.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Henry's Law:
\[ p = K_{\text{H}} \cdot x \implies x = \frac{p}{K_{\text{H}}} \]
Where \(x\) is mole fraction (solubility) in liquid. At a given partial pressure, solubility \(x\) is inversely proportional to Henry's law constant \(K_{\text{H}}\).

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compare the \(K_{\text{H}}\) values:
\[ K_{\text{H}}(\text{B}) < K_{\text{H}}(\text{C}) < K_{\text{H}}(\text{A}) \]
Taking reciprocals to derive solubility order:
\[ x(\text{B}) > x(\text{C}) > x(\text{A}) \implies \text{B} > \text{C} > \text{A} \]

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct solubility order in water is \(\text{B} > \text{C} > \text{A}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q78 - IUPAC name of C6H14 alkane with two tertiary carbons

questiontext.text: A compound with a molecular formula of \(\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}\) has two tertiary carbons. Its IUPAC name is:

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecular formula: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\)
Structural constraint: Exactly two tertiary (\(3^{\circ}\)) carbon atoms (carbons attached to three other carbons).

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard IUPAC nomenclature rules for branched alkanes.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Evaluate structural isomers of \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\):
- n-Hexane: Zero tertiary carbons.
- 2-Methylpentane: One tertiary carbon (C-2).
- 2,2-Dimethylbutane: One quaternary carbon (C-2) and zero tertiary carbons.
- 2,3-Dimethylbutane: \(\text{CH}_3\text{--}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{--}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{--}\text{CH}_3\).

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
In 2,3-dimethylbutane, C-2 is bonded to C-1, C-3, and a methyl group (tertiary carbon). Similarly, C-3 is bonded to C-2, C-4, and a methyl group (tertiary carbon).
Thus, 2,3-dimethylbutane possesses exactly two tertiary carbon atoms.

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The IUPAC name of the compound is 2,3-dimethylbutane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q79 - Equilibrium where Kp and Kc are not equal

questiontext.text: In which of the following equilibria, \(\mathrm{K_p}\) and \(\mathrm{K_c}\) are NOT equal?

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four gaseous equilibrium reactions.

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Ideal gas behavior applies to all reactants and products.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Relationship between \(K_{\text{p}}\) and \(K_{\text{c}}\):
\[ K_{\text{p}} = K_{\text{c}} (R T)^{\Delta n_{\text{g}}} \]
Where \(\Delta n_{\text{g}} = n_{\text{products(g)}} - n_{\text{reactants(g)}}\).
\(K_{\text{p}} = K_{\text{c}}\) if and only if \(\Delta n_{\text{g}} = 0\).

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(\Delta n_{\text{g}}\) for each equilibrium:
1. \(\text{CO}_{(\text{g})} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_{(\text{g})} \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_{2(\text{g})} + \text{H}_{2(\text{g})}\): \(\Delta n_{\text{g}} = (1+1) - (1+1) = 0 \implies K_{\text{p}} = K_{\text{c}}\).
2. \(2\text{BrCl}_{(\text{g})} \rightleftharpoons \text{Br}_{2(\text{g})} + \text{Cl}_{2(\text{g})}\): \(\Delta n_{\text{g}} = (1+1) - 2 = 0 \implies K_{\text{p}} = K_{\text{c}}\).
3. \(\text{PCl}_{5(\text{g})} \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_{3(\text{g})} + \text{Cl}_{2(\text{g})}\): \(\Delta n_{\text{g}} = (1+1) - 1 = +1 \neq 0 \implies K_{\text{p}} \neq K_{\text{c}}\).
4. \(\text{H}_{2(\text{g})} + \text{I}_{2(\text{g})} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}_{(\text{g})}\): \(\Delta n_{\text{g}} = 2 - (1+1) = 0 \implies K_{\text{p}} = K_{\text{c}}\).

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
\(K_{\text{p}}\) and \(K_{\text{c}}\) are not equal for the equilibrium \(\text{PCl}_{5(\text{g})} \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_{3(\text{g})} + \text{Cl}_{2(\text{g})}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q80 - Identification of non-redox precipitation reaction

questiontext.text: Which reaction is NOT a redox reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four chemical equations.

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A redox reaction requires at least one element to undergo a change in its formal oxidation state.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Assign oxidation states to all atoms across each reaction.

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \to 2\text{HCl}\): \(\text{H}^{(0)} \to \text{H}^{(+1)}\) and \(\text{Cl}^{(0)} \to \text{Cl}^{(-1)}\) (Redox).
2. \(\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{NaCl}\): Oxidation states are \(\text{Ba}^{(+2)}\), \(\text{Cl}^{(-1)}\), \(\text{Na}^{(+1)}\), \(\text{S}^{(+6)}\), \(\text{O}^{(-2)}\) on both reactant and product sides. Zero change in oxidation numbers occurs. This is a double displacement (precipitation) reaction.
3. \(\text{Zn} + \text{CuSO}_4 \to \text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{Cu}\): \(\text{Zn}^{(0)} \to \text{Zn}^{(+2)}\) and \(\text{Cu}^{(+2)} \to \text{Cu}^{(0)}\) (Redox).
4. \(2\text{KClO}_3 + \text{I}_2 \to 2\text{KIO}_3 + \text{Cl}_2\): \(\text{Cl}^{(+5)} \to \text{Cl}^{(0)}\) and \(\text{I}^{(0)} \to \text{I}^{(+5)}\) (Redox).

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The reaction \(\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{NaCl}\) is not a redox reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q81 - Magnetic behavior of cobalt III octahedral complexes

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I: Both \(\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_6\right]^{3+}\) and \(\left[\mathrm{CoF}_6\right]^{3-}\) complexes are octahedral but differ in their magnetic behaviour.

Statement II: \(\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_6\right]^{3+}\) is diamagnetic whereas \(\left[\mathrm{CoF}_6\right]^{3-}\) is paramagnetic.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Crystal Field Theory states that ligand strength determines whether $d$-electrons pair up (low-spin/diamagnetic) or remain unpaired (high-spin/paramagnetic) in octahedral complexes.

Evaluation of Statements
In both \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\) and \([\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}\), cobalt is in $+3$ oxidation state (\(3d^6\)) with coordination number 6, forming octahedral complexes.
- In \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\), \(\text{NH}_3\) is a strong field ligand, causing strong crystal field splitting (\(\Delta_{\text{o}} > P\)). All six \(3d\) electrons pair up in the \(t_{2\text{g}}\) orbitals (\(t_{2\text{g}}^6 e_{\text{g}}^0\)), giving zero unpaired electrons (\(n = 0\)), making the complex diamagnetic.
- In \([\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}\), \(\text{F}^-\) is a weak field ligand (\(\Delta_{\text{o}} < P\)). Electrons do not pair up (\(t_{2\text{g}}^4 e_{\text{g}}^2\)), giving four unpaired electrons (\(n = 4\)), making the complex paramagnetic.
Therefore, Statement I is true and Statement II is true.

Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

answer.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_SECTIONA_Q82 - Mass of unreacted sodium hydroxide in neutralization

questiontext.text: 1 gram of sodium hydroxide was treated with 25 mL of 0.75 M HCl solution, the mass of sodium hydroxide left unreacted is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Stage 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial mass of \(\text{NaOH}\): \(m_{\text{initial}} = 1\ \text{g}\)
Volume of \(\text{HCl}\) solution: \(V = 25\ \text{mL} = 0.025\ \text{L}\)
Molarity of \(\text{HCl}\) solution: \(M = 0.75\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\)
Molar mass of \(\text{NaOH}\): \(40\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Stage 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Neutralization reaction goes to completion according to 1:1 stoichiometry.

Stage 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Chemical equation:
\[ \text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \to \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \]
Moles of \(\text{NaOH}\) initial: \(n_1 = \frac{m}{M_{\text{w}}}\)
Moles of \(\text{HCl}\) added: \(n_2 = M \times V\)

Stage 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate initial moles of \(\text{NaOH}\):
\[ n_1 = \frac{1\ \text{g}}{40\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.025\ \text{mol} = 25\ \text{mmol} \]
2. Calculate moles of \(\text{HCl}\) added:
\[ n_2 = 0.75\ \text{mol L}^{-1} \times 0.025\ \text{L} = 0.01875\ \text{mol} = 18.75\ \text{mmol} \]
3. Calculate unreacted moles of \(\text{NaOH}\):
\[ n_{\text{unreacted}} = 25\ \text{mmol} - 18.75\ \text{mmol} = 6.25\ \text{mmol} = 0.00625\ \text{mol} \]
4. Calculate unreacted mass of \(\text{NaOH}\):
\[ m_{\text{unreacted}} = 0.00625\ \text{mol} \times 40\ \text{g mol}^{-1} = 0.25\ \text{g} = 250\ \text{mg} \]

Stage 5: Check and Final Answer
The mass of sodium hydroxide left unreacted is \(250\ \text{mg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_A_Q83 - Group 16 element with no negative two oxidation state

questiontext.text: Among Group 16 elements, which one does NOT show \(-2\) oxidation state?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Group 16 elements (Oxygen, Sulfur, Selenium, Tellurium, and Polonium) exhibit various oxidation states. Non-metals and metalloids in this group readily display a \(-2\) oxidation state when bonding with more electropositive elements, such as in hydrides (\(\text{H}_2\text{E}\)).

Evaluation
Polonium is a radioactive metal situated at the bottom of Group 16. Because of its pronounced metallic character and lower electronegativity, polonium does not show a negative oxidation state of \(-2\).

Final Conclusion
The element in Group 16 that does not exhibit a \(-2\) oxidation state is polonium (\(\text{Po}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_A_Q84 - Identification of processes in which entropy increases

questiontext.text:
In which of the following processes entropy increases?

A. A liquid evaporates to vapour.
B. Temperature of a crystalline solid lowered from \(130\text{ K}\) to \(0\text{ K}\).
C. \(2\text{NaHCO}_{3(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_{3(s)} + \text{CO}_{2(g)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_{(g)}\)
D. \(\text{Cl}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}_{(g)}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Entropy (\(S\)) is a measure of randomness or molecular disorder in a system. Any physical or chemical transition that increases the freedom of movement, number of gaseous moles, or number of particles leads to an increase in entropy (\(\Delta S > 0\)).

Evaluation of Statements
- Phase transition from liquid to vapour involves a transition to a highly disordered state with greater molecular motion, leading to an increase in entropy.
- Lowering the temperature of a crystalline solid reduces vibrational and thermal kinetic energy of atoms, which causes a decrease in entropy.
- Thermal decomposition of solid sodium bicarbonate yields 1 mole of solid product along with 2 moles of gaseous products (\(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)). The formation of gaseous moles from a solid reactant increases randomness significantly.
- Dissociation of 1 mole of diatomic chlorine gas into 2 moles of gaseous chlorine atoms increases the total number of particles and accessible microstates, resulting in an entropy increase.

Final Conclusion
Entropy increases in processes A, C, and D.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_A_Q85 - Faraday required for chemical conversions in electrochemistry

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II.

List I (Conversion)
A. \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) to \(\text{O}_2\)
B. \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\)
C. \(1.5\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Ca}\) from molten \(\text{CaCl}_2\)
D. \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{FeO}\) to \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\)

List II (Number of Faraday required)
I. \(3\text{F}\)
II. \(2\text{F}\)
III. \(1\text{F}\)
IV. \(5\text{F}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- Oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) to \(\text{O}_2\).
- Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\).
- Electrolytic deposition of \(1.5\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Ca}\) from molten \(\text{CaCl}_2\).
- Oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{FeO}\) to \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\).

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- \(1\text{ mole}\) of electrons carries a charge of \(1\text{ Faraday } (1\text{F})\).
- Reaction stoichiometry determines the exact electron transfer.

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Total electric charge in Faraday: \(Q = n \cdot F\), where \(n\) is the number of moles of electrons transferred.

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- For oxidation of water: \(2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^-\). Here \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) require \(4\text{F}\), so \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) requires \(\frac{4}{2} = 2\text{F}\) (matches II).
- For reduction of permanganate ion: \(\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\). Oxidation state of Mn decreases from \(+7\) to \(+2\), requiring \(5\text{ mol}\) of electrons (\(5\text{F}\)) per mole of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) (matches IV).
- For reduction of calcium ions: \(\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Ca}\). Production of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Ca}\) requires \(2\text{F}\). Producing \(1.5\text{ mol}\) requires \(1.5 \times 2 = 3\text{F}\) (matches I).
- For oxidation of iron(II) oxide: \(\text{FeO} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\). Oxidation state of Fe increases from \(+2\) to \(+3\), transferring \(1\text{ mol}\) of electron (\(1\text{F}\)) per mole of \(\text{FeO}\) (matches III).

5. Check and Final Answer:
The correct match sequence is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q86 - Major products in bromination followed by elimination sequence

questiontext.text: Major products A and B formed in the following reaction sequence, are

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- Reactant: 2-methylcyclohexanol.
- Reagents: \(\text{PBr}_3\) in step 1; \(\text{alcoholic KOH}, \Delta\) in step 2.

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- Nucleophilic substitution with \(\text{PBr}_3\) replaces hydroxyl with bromide.
- Elimination with alcoholic KOH under heating follows Zaitsev's rule to produce the most substituted alkene.

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- \(S_N2\) halogenation of alcohols using phosphorus tribromide (\(\text{PBr}_3\)).
- Zaitsev's rule: Dehydrohalogenation yields the more highly substituted, thermodynamically stable alkene as the major product.

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- In step 1, 2-methylcyclohexanol reacts with \(\text{PBr}_3\) to replace the hydroxyl group (\(-\text{OH}\)) with a bromine atom (\(-\text{Br}\)), yielding 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane as product A.
- In step 2, treatment of 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane with alcoholic \(\text{KOH}\) under heating induces an \(E2\) elimination.
- Removal of a proton from the more substituted adjacent carbon (C1) bearing the methyl group forms the tetrasubstituted alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene, as major product B.

5. Check and Final Answer:
Product A is 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane and product B is 1-methylcyclohexene, matching the structures illustrated in the third option set.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q87 - Degree of dissociation from equilibrium constant

questiontext.text: For the equilibrium reaction \(2\text{NO}_{(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{N}_{2(g)} + \text{O}_{2(g)}\), the equilibrium concentrations are \([\text{NO}] = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\), \([\text{N}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\), and \([\text{O}_2] = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\). The degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) of \(\text{NO}\) is approximately:

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- \([\text{NO}] = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\)
- \([\text{N}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\)
- \([\text{O}_2] = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\)

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- Reversible gas-phase equilibrium reaction.
- Initial concentration of reactant is \(C_0\), and degree of dissociation is \(\alpha\).

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Equilibrium constant expression: \(K_c = \frac{[\text{N}_2][\text{O}_2]}{[\text{NO}]^2}\)
- For dissociation of \(2\text{NO} \rightleftharpoons \text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2\):
\([\text{NO}] = C_0(1-\alpha)\), \([\text{N}_2] = \frac{C_0 \alpha}{2}\), \([\text{O}_2] = \frac{C_0 \alpha}{2}\)
\(K_c = \frac{\alpha^2}{4(1-\alpha)^2}\)

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- Calculate equilibrium constant \(K_c\):
\[K_c = \frac{(3.0 \times 10^{-3})(4.2 \times 10^{-3})}{(2.8 \times 10^{-3})^2} = \frac{12.6 \times 10^{-6}}{7.84 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.607\]
- Express \(\alpha\) in terms of \(K_c\):
\[\frac{\alpha}{2(1-\alpha)} = \sqrt{1.607} \approx 1.2677\]
\[\alpha = 2.535(1-\alpha) = 2.535 - 2.535\alpha\]
\[3.535\alpha = 2.535 \implies \alpha = \frac{2.535}{3.535} \approx 0.717\]

5. Check and Final Answer:
The degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) is approximately \(0.717\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q88 - Phosphorus products in alcohol reactions with PCl3 and PCl5

questiontext.text:
Identify A and B in the following reaction sequence:

\[3\text{ROH} + \text{PCl}_3 \rightarrow 3\text{RCl} + \text{A}\]

\[\text{ROH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{RCl} + \text{B} + \text{HCl}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Reactions of alcohols with phosphorus halides are standard synthetic methods for preparing alkyl halides. Phosphorus trichloride (\(\text{PCl}_3\)) and phosphorus pentachloride (\(\text{PCl}_5\)) act as chlorinating agents, producing distinct inorganic side-products.

Evaluation
- Reaction of 3 moles of alcohol with phosphorus trichloride generates 3 moles of alkyl chloride along with 1 mole of phosphorous acid (\(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\)). Therefore, compound A is \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\).
- Reaction of alcohol with phosphorus pentachloride yields alkyl chloride, hydrogen chloride, and phosphorus oxychloride (\(\text{POCl}_3\)). Therefore, compound B is \(\text{POCl}_3\).

Final Conclusion
Compound A is \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\) and compound B is \(\text{POCl}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q89 - Group number ordering in qualitative inorganic analysis

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following cations in the increasing order of their Group number in qualitative inorganic analysis:

A. \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\)
B. \(\text{Al}^{3+}\)
C. \(\text{Co}^{2+}\)
D. \(\text{Ba}^{2+}\)
E. \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In qualitative inorganic salt analysis, cations are classified into groups based on the solubility products of their salts precipitated by specific group reagents.

Evaluation
- \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) belongs to Group II (precipitated as sulfide in acidic medium).
- \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) belongs to Group III (precipitated as hydroxide by ammonium hydroxide in presence of ammonium chloride).
- \(\text{Co}^{2+}\) belongs to Group IV (precipitated as sulfide in alkaline medium).
- \(\text{Ba}^{2+}\) belongs to Group V (precipitated as carbonate).
- \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) belongs to Group VI (zero group / final group cations).

Final Conclusion
The increasing order of cations by Group number is A, B, C, D, E.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q90 - Role of dilute sulfuric acid in Mohr salt preparation

questiontext.text: In the preparation of Mohr's salt, dilute sulfuric acid is added to prevent:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Mohr's salt is ferrous ammonium sulfate, \(\text{FeSO}_4 \cdot (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\). In aqueous solutions, salts of weak bases and strong acids tend to undergo cationic hydrolysis.

Evaluation
Ferrous sulfate (\(\text{FeSO}_4\)) undergoes hydrolysis in water to produce insoluble basic ferrous salts/hydroxides, causing turbidity in solution. Adding dilute sulfuric acid increases \(\text{H}^+\) concentration in the medium, shifting the hydrolysis equilibrium backward and preventing hydrolysis of ferrous ions (\(\text{Fe}^{2+}\)).

Final Conclusion
Dilute sulfuric acid is added to prevent the hydrolysis of ferrous sulfate.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q91 - Reversible isothermal expansion work of ideal gas

questiontext.text: Calculate the maximum work done in calories during the isothermal reversible expansion of \(1\text{ mole}\) of an ideal gas (\(\text{H}_2\)) at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) from a pressure of \(20\text{ atm}\) to \(10\text{ atm}\). (Given: \(R = 2.0\text{ cal K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), \(\log 2 = 0.3010\))

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- Moles of gas, \(n = 1\text{ mol}\)
- Temperature, \(T = 25^\circ\text{C} = 298\text{ K}\)
- Initial pressure, \(P_1 = 20\text{ atm}\)
- Final pressure, \(P_2 = 10\text{ atm}\)
- Gas constant, \(R = 2.0\text{ cal K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
- \(\log 2 = 0.3010\)

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- The gas behaves ideally and undergoes reversible isothermal expansion.
- Work done by the system is negative according to IUPAC convention: \(W = -2.303 n R T \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)\).

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Isothermal reversible work formula in terms of pressure:
\[W = -2.303 n R T \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)\]

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- Substitute the values:
\[W = -2.303 \times 1\text{ mol} \times 2.0\text{ cal K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} \times 298\text{ K} \times \log_{10}\left(\frac{20}{10}\right)\]
\[W = -2.303 \times 2.0 \times 298 \times \log_{10}(2)\]
\[W = -2.303 \times 596 \times 0.3010\]
\[W = -1372.588 \times 0.3010 \approx -413.14\text{ cal}\]

5. Check and Final Answer:
The calculated work done is \(-413.14\text{ calories}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q92 - Oxidative cleavage of internal alkyne with KMnO4

questiontext.text: Identify product P in the following reaction:

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- Reactant: dicyclohexylethyne (a symmetrical internal alkyne).
- Reagent: \(\text{KMnO}_4 / \text{H}^+, \Delta\).

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- Vigorous oxidation with hot acidic potassium permanganate causes complete cleavage of the carbon-carbon triple bond.

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Oxidative cleavage of internal alkynes (\(\text{R-C}\equiv\text{C-R}\)) with acidic \(\text{KMnO}_4\) cleaves the triple bond to produce carboxylic acids (\(\text{R-COOH}\)).

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- The reactant contains two cyclohexyl rings linked by an ethyne bridge (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\)).
- Acidic \(\text{KMnO}_4\) under thermal conditions breaks the triple bond completely.
- Each acetylenic carbon is oxidized to a carboxylic acid group, converting the molecule into 2 moles of cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{COOH}\)).

5. Check and Final Answer:
The product P is cyclohexanecarboxylic acid, corresponding to the fourth structure provided in the options.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q93 - Temperature determination from osmotic pressure slope

questiontext.text: A plot of osmotic pressure (\(\Pi\)) vs concentration (\(C\)) for a solution of a solute at temperature \(T\) gives a straight line passing through the origin with a slope of \(25.73\text{ L bar mol}^{-1}\). The temperature \(T\) of the solution in Celsius is: (Given: \(R = 0.083\text{ L bar K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- Slope of \(\Pi\) vs \(C\) plot = \(25.73\text{ L bar mol}^{-1}\)
- Universal gas constant, \(R = 0.083\text{ L bar K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- The solution follows van 't Hoff's osmotic pressure law for dilute solutions.

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Osmotic pressure equation: \(\Pi = C R T\)
- A plot of \(\Pi\) against \(C\) gives a straight line with slope equal to \(R T\).

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- Equate the slope to \(R T\):
\[\text{Slope} = R T = 25.73\text{ L bar mol}^{-1}\]
- Solve for absolute temperature \(T\):
\[T = \frac{25.73}{0.083} = 310\text{ K}\]
- Convert temperature to Celsius scale:
\[t(^\circ\text{C}) = 310 - 273 = 37^\circ\text{C}\]

5. Check and Final Answer:
The calculated temperature in Celsius is \(37^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q94 - Major product C in nitrile hydrolysis and Hofmann degradation sequence

questiontext.text:
In the following reaction sequence:

\[\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{I} \xrightarrow{\text{NaCN}} \text{A} \xrightarrow{\text{OH}^- / \text{partial hydrolysis}} \text{B} \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2 / \text{NaOH}} \text{C}\]

The major product C formed is:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
This multi-step synthesis involves nucleophilic substitution of an alkyl halide to form a nitrile, partial hydrolysis of the nitrile to an amide, and Hofmann bromamide degradation of the primary amide to yield a primary amine containing one fewer carbon atom.

Evaluation of Reaction Steps
- Step 1: Reaction of 1-iodopropane with \(\text{NaCN}\) yields butyronitrile (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}\)) as intermediate A.
- Step 2: Partial alkaline hydrolysis of butyronitrile converts the nitrile group (\(-\text{CN}\)) to an amide group (\(-\text{CONH}_2\)), forming butanamide (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2\)) as intermediate B.
- Step 3: Treatment of butanamide with \(\text{Br}_2\) and \(\text{NaOH}\) undergoes Hofmann degradation, eliminating the carbonyl carbon and converting the amide into propan-1-amine (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\)) as final product C.

Final Conclusion
The major product C is propan-1-amine (\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q95 - Empirical formula calculation from mass percentage composition

questiontext.text: A compound contains \(32\%\) of element A, \(20\%\) of element B, and \(48\%\) of element C by mass. If the atomic masses of A, B, and C are \(64\), \(40\), and \(32\) respectively, the empirical formula of the compound is:

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- Mass percentage of element A = \(32\%\), atomic mass = \(64\)
- Mass percentage of element B = \(20\%\), atomic mass = \(40\)
- Mass percentage of element C = \(48\%\), atomic mass = \(32\)

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- Assume a total compound mass of \(100\text{ g}\).

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Moles of an element: \(n = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Atomic Mass}}\)
- Empirical formula ratio is obtained by dividing the moles of each element by the smallest mole value among them.

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- Moles of A: \(n_A = \frac{32}{64} = 0.5\)
- Moles of B: \(n_B = \frac{20}{40} = 0.5\)
- Moles of C: \(n_C = \frac{48}{32} = 1.5\)
- Simplest molar ratio relative to \(0.5\):
\[\text{Ratio for A} = \frac{0.5}{0.5} = 1\]
\[\text{Ratio for B} = \frac{0.5}{0.5} = 1\]
\[\text{Ratio for C} = \frac{1.5}{0.5} = 3\]
- The whole number mole ratio A : B : C is 1 : 1 : 3.

5. Check and Final Answer:
The empirical formula of the compound is \(\text{ABC}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_T1_SECTION_B_Q96 - Activation energy calculation from Arrhenius equation

questiontext.text: The rate of a reaction quadruples when the temperature changes from \(27^\circ\text{C}\) to \(57^\circ\text{C}\). The activation energy (\(E_a\)) for the reaction is: (Given: \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), \(\log 4 = 0.6021\))

generalfeedback.text:
1. Given Data and Conditions:
- \(T_1 = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300\text{ K}\)
- \(T_2 = 57^\circ\text{C} = 330\text{ K}\)
- Rate constant ratio, \(\frac{k_2}{k_1} = 4\)
- Universal gas constant, \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
- \(\log 4 = 0.6021\)

2. Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
- The activation energy \(E_a\) remains independent of temperature over this temperature range.

3. Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- Arrhenius equation:
\[\log_{10}\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left(\frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right)\]

4. Step-by-Step Working:
- Substitute the known values:
\[0.6021 = \frac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \left(\frac{330 - 300}{300 \times 330}\right)\]
\[0.6021 = \frac{E_a}{19.147} \left(\frac{30}{99000}\right)\]
\[0.6021 = \frac{E_a}{19.147 \times 3300}\]
\[E_a = 0.6021 \times 19.147 \times 3300\]
\[E_a = 38043.7\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx 38.04\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

5. Check and Final Answer:
The calculated activation energy is \(38.04\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_Q97 - Canonical forms and dipole moment of molecules

questiontext.text: Identify the correct answer.

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Resonance structure feasibility and dipole moment magnitudes depend on molecular geometry and symmetry.

Evaluation of Statements
- Carbonate ion (\(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\)) has three equivalent canonical (resonance) structures.
- Nitrogen trifluoride (\(\text{NF}_3\)) has a dipole moment (\(0.24\text{ D}\)) smaller than ammonia (\(\text{NH}_3\), \(1.47\text{ D}\)) because the unshared electron pair dipole opposes the resultant dipole of the three \(\text{N}-\text{F}\) bonds.
- Ozone (\(\text{O}_3\)) has two major canonical resonance structures.
- Boron trifluoride (\(\text{BF}_3\)) has a symmetrical trigonal planar geometry, resulting in a net zero dipole moment.

Final Conclusion
The assertion that three canonical forms can be drawn for the carbonate ion is correct.

answer.text: Dipole moment of \(\text{NF}_3\) is greater than that of \(\text{NH}_3\).
Three canonical forms can be drawn for \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) ion.
Three resonance structures can be drawn for ozone.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_Q98 - Identification of diamagnetic lanthanoid ions

questiontext.text: The pair of lanthanoid ions which are diamagnetic is

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A species is diamagnetic if all of its electrons are paired and its \(4f\) subshell contains either 0 or 14 electrons (\(4f^0\) or \(4f^{14}\)). Species with partially filled \(4f\) subshells contain unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic.

Evaluation of Electronic Configurations
- Cerium(IV) ion (\(\text{Ce}^{4+}\)): Atomic number of Cerium is 58. Neutral Cerium has configuration \([\text{Xe}] 4f^1 5d^1 6s^2\). Upon losing 4 electrons, \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\) acquires \([\text{Xe}] 4f^0\) configuration with zero unpaired electrons, making it diamagnetic.
- Ytterbium(II) ion (\(\text{Yb}^{2+}\)): Atomic number of Ytterbium is 70. Neutral Ytterbium has configuration \([\text{Xe}] 4f^{14} 6s^2\). Upon losing 2 electrons, \(\text{Yb}^{2+}\) acquires \([\text{Xe}] 4f^{14}\) configuration with a completely filled \(4f\) subshell and zero unpaired electrons, making it diamagnetic.
- Other ions such as \(\text{Gd}^{3+}\) (\(4f^7\)), \(\text{Eu}^{3+}\) (\(4f^6\)), \(\text{Pm}^{3+}\) (\(4f^4\)), \(\text{Sm}^{3+}\) (\(4f^5\)), \(\text{Ce}^{3+}\) (\(4f^1\)), and \(\text{Eu}^{2+}\) (\(4f^7\)) all possess unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic.

Final Conclusion
The pair consisting of \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\) and \(\text{Yb}^{2+}\) is diamagnetic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_Q99 - Homoleptic and heteroleptic cobalt complexes

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : \(\left[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6\right]^{3+}\) is a homoleptic complex whereas \(\left[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2\right]^+\) is a heteroleptic complex.

Statement II : Complex \(\left[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6\right]^{3+}\) has only one kind of ligands but \(\left[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2\right]^+\) has more than one kind of ligands.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Complexes in which a metal ion is bound to only one type of donor group are termed homoleptic complexes. Complexes in which a metal ion is bound to more than one type of donor group are termed heteroleptic complexes.

Evaluation of Statements
- In \(\left[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6\right]^{3+}\), the central cobalt ion is bound solely to six ammine (\(\text{NH}_3\)) ligands of one type. Hence, it is a homoleptic complex.
- In \(\left[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2\right]^+\), the cobalt ion is bound to two different types of ligands: four ammine ligands and two chloride ligands. Hence, it is a heteroleptic complex.
- Therefore, the assertion classifying these complexes as homoleptic and heteroleptic respectively is true, and the explanation stating that one has a single kind of ligand while the other has multiple kinds of ligands is also true.

Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

answer.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2024_Q100 - Mass of copper deposited by electrolysis

questiontext.text:
Mass in grams of copper deposited by passing 9.6487 A current through a voltmeter containing copper sulphate solution for 100 seconds is:

(Given : Molar mass of Cu : 63 g mol-1, 1F = 96487 C)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current (\(I\)) = \(9.6487\text{ A}\)
Time (\(t\)) = \(100\text{ s}\)
Molar mass of \(\text{Cu}\) (\(M\)) = \(63\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)
Faraday constant (\(F\)) = \(96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the total charge passed is:
\[Q = I \times t\]
The cathodic reduction of copper is:
\[\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}\]
Thus, \(n = 2\) moles of electrons deposit 1 mole (\(63\text{ g}\)) of copper.
The mass of copper deposited is:
\[m = \frac{M \times Q}{n \times F} = \frac{M \times I \times t}{n \times F}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate total electric charge passed:
\[Q = 9.6487\text{ A} \times 100\text{ s} = 964.87\text{ C}\]
Substitute values into the mass formula:
\[m = \frac{63\text{ g mol}^{-1} \times 964.87\text{ C}}{2 \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}}\]
Notice that \(\frac{964.87}{96487} = 10^{-2}\):
\[m = \frac{63 \times 10^{-2}}{2} = 31.5 \times 10^{-2} = 0.315\text{ g}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The mass of copper deposited by \(964.87\text{ C}\) is \(0.315\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q101 - Component of stomata with thick inner walls

questiontext.text: In the given figure, which component has thin outer walls and highly thickened inner walls?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Diagram Interpretation
The diagram illustrates a stomatal complex in surface view, showing the stomatal pore, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary and epidermal cells.
Labels in the diagram:
- A indicates subsidiary/epidermal cells.
- B indicates the body of the guard cell.
- C indicates the inner thick wall of the guard cell surrounding the stomatal aperture.
- D indicates the stomatal pore/aperture.

Step 2: Relevant Principles
In plant stomata, the guard cells have outer walls (away from the pore) that are thin and flexible, while the inner walls (facing the stomatal pore) are highly thickened. This differential wall thickening allows guard cells to bulge outward when turgid, opening the pore.

Step 3: Evaluation
Label C specifically highlights the inner thickened cell wall of the guard cells facing the pore.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The component with thin outer walls and highly thickened inner walls is represented by label C.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q102 - Organization releasing list of endangered species

questiontext.text: List of endangered species was released by-

generalfeedback.text:

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), headquartered in Gland, Switzerland, maintains and releases the Red List of Threatened Species, evaluating the conservation status of species globally to highlight those facing extinction risks.

Evaluation of Organizations

- FOAM refers to Friends of the Arcata Marsh, involved in integrated wastewater treatment.
- GEAC (Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee) evaluates research and safety of genetically modified organisms in India.

The list of endangered species is released by IUCN.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q103 - Protection of species outside natural habitat

questiontext.text: The type of conservation in which the threatened species are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special setting where they can be protected and given special care is called;

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity conservation strategies are broadly categorized into in-situ (on-site) conservation and ex-situ (off-site) conservation.

Evaluation of Conservation Methods
- Removing threatened animal or plant species from their natural habitat and placing them in human-controlled settings (such as botanical gardens, zoological parks, cryopreservation facilities, or safari parks) where they receive intensive protection is specifically termed ex-situ conservation, which is an integral component of biodiversity conservation.
- Protecting species within their natural environment (such as national parks, biosphere reserves, and sanctuaries) is termed in-situ conservation.

Final Conclusion
This approach is classified under biodiversity conservation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q104 - Features explained by Law of Dominance

questiontext.text:
Which one of the following can be explained on the basis of Mendel's Law of Dominance?

A. Out of one pair of factors one is dominant and the other is recessive.
B. Alleles do not show any expression and both the characters appear as such in \(\text{F}_2\) generation.
C. Factors occur in pairs in normal diploid plants.
D. The discrete unit controlling a particular character is called factor.
E. The expression of only one of the parental characters is found in a monohybrid cross.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Mendel's Law of Dominance states three primary postulates:
1. Characters are controlled by discrete units called factors.
2. Factors occur in pairs.
3. In a dissimilar pair of factors, one member of the pair dominates (dominant) the other (recessive).
This law explains why only one parental trait is expressed in the F1 generation of a monohybrid cross while both traits appear in the F2 generation.

Evaluation of Statements
- Statement A: Describes dominant and recessive factors in a dissimilar pair (Law of Dominance).
- Statement B: States that alleles do not blend and segregate so both traits reappear in F2. This is explained by Mendel's Law of Segregation, not Dominance.
- Statement C: States that factors occur in pairs in diploid plants (Law of Dominance).
- Statement D: States that discrete units controlling characters are called factors (Law of Dominance).
- Statement E: Explains that only one parental trait appears in F1 in a monohybrid cross (Law of Dominance).

Final Conclusion
Statements A, C, D, and E are explained on the basis of Mendel's Law of Dominance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q105 - Transport of lactose in bacterial cell

questiontext.text: The lactose present in the growth medium of bacteria is transported to the cell by the action of:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In the lac operon of Escherichia coli, the structural genes lacZ, lacY, and lacA encode enzymes involved in lactose metabolism.

Enzymatic Roles
- Permease (encoded by lacY) increases permeability of the cell membrane to \(\beta\)-galactosides, enabling entry of lactose into the bacterial cell.
- \(\beta\)-galactosidase (encoded by lacZ) hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose.
- Transacetylase (encoded by lacA) transfers an acetyl group to \(\beta\)-galactosides.
- Polymerase synthesizes nucleic acids (DNA/RNA).

Final Conclusion
Lactose is transported into the bacterial cell by the action of Permease.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q107 - Parameter K in logistic growth equation

questiontext.text:
The equation of Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth is

\[\frac{dN}{dt} = rN \left[ \frac{K-N}{K} \right]\]

From this equation, K indicates:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth model describes population growth in an environment with limited resources.

Parameters of the Logistic Equation
In the equation \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN \left[ \frac{K-N}{K} \right]\):
- \(N\) represents population density at time \(t\).
- \(r\) represents the intrinsic rate of natural increase.
- \(K\) represents the carrying capacity, which is the maximum population size that a given habitat can sustain with its available resources.

Final Conclusion
The symbol K indicates the Carrying capacity.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q108 - Three primary regions of transcription unit

questiontext.text: A transcription unit in DNA is defined primarily by the three regions in DNA and these are with respect to upstream and downstream end;

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A transcription unit is a sequence of DNA that is transcribed into an RNA molecule.

Structural Regions of Transcription Unit
A transcription unit consists of three functional regions:
1. Promoter: Located upstream (towards the 5'-end of the coding strand), providing binding site for RNA polymerase.
2. Structural gene: The region flanked by promoter and terminator that encodes RNA.
3. Terminator: Located downstream (towards the 3'-end of the coding strand), defining the end of transcription.

Final Conclusion
The three defined regions are Promoter, Structural gene, and Terminator.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q109 - Interfascicular cambium formation as dedifferentiation

questiontext.text: Formation of interfascicular cambium from fully developed parenchyma cells is an example for

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In plant growth, cellular development undergoes differentiation, dedifferentiation, and redifferentiation.

Developmental Definitions
- Differentiation: The process where meristematic cells undergo structural and functional specialization.
- Dedifferentiation: The process where living, fully differentiated cells that have lost the capacity to divide regain meristematic capability under specific conditions.
- Redifferentiation: The process where dedifferentiated meristematic cells divide and mature into specialized tissues again.

Parenchyma cells are mature, fully differentiated tissues. When medullary ray parenchyma cells between vascular bundles regain division capacity to form interfascicular cambium, they undergo dedifferentiation.

Final Conclusion
This process is an example of Dedifferentiation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q111 - Fate of isolated alien gene fragment

questiontext.text:
What is the fate of a piece of DNA carrying only gene of interest which is transferred into an alien organism?

A. The piece of DNA would be able to multiply itself independently in the progeny cells of the organism.
B. It may get integrated into the genome of the recipient.
C. It may multiply and be inherited along with the host DNA.
D. The alien piece of DNA is not an integral part of chromosome.
E. It shows ability to replicate.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
For a DNA fragment to replicate inside a host organism, it must possess an origin of replication sequence (ori).

Evaluation of Statements
- An isolated piece of DNA lacking an origin of replication cannot replicate independently in recipient cells.
- When integrated into the recipient host's chromosome/genome, it utilizes the host cell's origin of replication, thereby multiplying and being inherited alongside host chromosomal DNA (Statements B and C are correct).
- Statements A, D, and E are incorrect because without integration or a functional vector with an origin of replication, the alien DNA cannot replicate or persist autonomously.

Final Conclusion
Statements B and C only correctly state the fate of the transferred DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q112 - Matching cell organelles with primary functions

Conceptual Principle
Cellular organelles perform specific structural and metabolic functions within eukaryotic cells.

- Centriole consists of nine evenly spaced peripheral triplets of tubulin fibrils, exhibiting a cartwheel-like organization (B matches II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q113 - Floral position of ovary in plum and rose

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Based on the position of calyx, corolla, and androecium with respect to the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are classified as hypogynous, perigynous, or epigynous.

Evaluation of Figures
- In perigynous flowers, the gynoecium is situated in the center and other floral parts are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level. The ovary in such flowers is half-inferior, as seen in plum, rose, and peach.
- Both figures (a) and (b) illustrate perigynous flowers where the thalamus forms a cup-shaped structure surrounding the half-inferior ovary with calyx, corolla, and stamens attached at the rim.

Final Conclusion
Both figure (a) and figure (b) represent perigynous flowers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q114 - Spindle fiber attachment during cell division

questiontext.text: Spindle fibers attach to kinetochores of chromosomes during

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Mitotic cell division progresses through prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.

Phase Characteristics
- During metaphase, condensation of chromosomes is complete, and spindle fibers attach to the disc-shaped kinetochores located on the centromeres of chromosomes, aligning them at the equatorial metaphase plate.
- During prophase, chromatin condenses and the mitotic spindle begins to assemble.
- During anaphase, centromeres split and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
- During telophase, nuclear envelopes reform around daughter chromosome sets.

Final Conclusion
Spindle fibers attach to kinetochores during Metaphase.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q115 - Major drivers of biodiversity loss

questiontext.text:
These are regarded as major causes of biodiversity loss:

A. Over exploitation
B. Co-extinction
C. Mutation
D. Habitat loss and fragmentation
E. Migration

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Accelerated rates of species extinction worldwide are driven primarily by human activities, collectively termed 'The Evil Quartet'.

Evaluation of Factors
- The four major causes of biodiversity loss are:
1. Habitat loss and fragmentation (D)
2. Over-exploitation (A)
3. Alien species invasions
4. Co-extinctions (B)
- Mutation (C) is a source of genetic variation, and migration (E) is a natural movement process, neither of which is a major driver of biodiversity loss.

Final Conclusion
The major causes of biodiversity loss are Over-exploitation, Co-extinction, and Habitat loss and fragmentation (A, B and D only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q116 - Chemical classification of lecithin

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q117 - Features of water pollination in aquatic plants

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q118 - Metal cofactor for carboxypeptidase

questiontext.text: The cofactor of the enzyme carboxypeptidase is:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Cofactors are non-protein constituents bound to enzymes that render them catalytically active. Metal ions act as cofactors by forming coordination bonds with side chains at the active site.

Enzyme Cofactors

- Haem is a prosthetic group for enzymes like peroxidase and catalase.
- Flavin and Niacin form coenzymes (FAD/FMN and NAD/NADP respectively).

The cofactor of carboxypeptidase is Zinc.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q119 - Competitive inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase

questiontext.text: Inhibition of Succinic dehydrogenase enzyme by malonate is a classical example of:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
When an inhibitor closely resembles the substrate in its molecular structure and competes for the active site of an enzyme, the process is called competitive inhibition.

Enzymatic Analysis
- Succinic dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate.
- Malonate closely resembles succinate in structure and binds to the active site of succinic dehydrogenase without being converted to product, thereby inhibiting enzymatic activity.

Final Conclusion
The inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase by malonate is a classic example of Competitive inhibition.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q120 - Identification of actinomorphic floral symmetry

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of actinomorphic flower?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Flowers showing radial symmetry (can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the center) are actinomorphic. Flowers showing bilateral symmetry (can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane) are zygomorphic.

Symmetry Classification
- Datura, Mustard, and Chilli exhibit actinomorphic symmetry.
- Pisum (pea), Sesbania, and Cassia (as well as bean and gulmohar) exhibit zygomorphic symmetry.

Final Conclusion
Datura possesses actinomorphic flowers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q121 - Meiotic prophase I stages leptotene and diplotene

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I : Chromosomes become gradually visible under light microscope during leptotene stage.

Statement II : The beginning of diplotene stage is recognized by dissolution of synaptonemal complex.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Prophase I of meiotic division consists of five substages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, and diakinesis.

Evaluation of Statements
- Statement I: During leptotene, compaction of chromatin continues and chromosomes become gradually visible under a light microscope (True).
- Statement II: Diplotene is marked by the dissolution of the synaptonemal complex and the tendency of homologous chromosomes to separate, remaining attached only at chiasmata (True).

Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

answer.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q122 - Incomplete dominance inheritance in snapdragon cross

questiontext.text: A pink flowered Snapdragon plant was crossed with a red flowered Snapdragon plant. What type of phenotype/s is/are expected in the progeny?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Genetics Model
In Snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus), flower color exhibits incomplete dominance:
- Homozygous red flower genotype = \(RR\)
- Homozygous white flower genotype = \(rr\)
- Heterozygous pink flower genotype = \(Rr\)

Step 2: Cross Working
Cross between pink flowered (\(Rr\)) and red flowered (\(RR\)) plants:
\[Rr \times RR\]
Gametes produced:
- Pink parent: \(R\) and \(r\)
- Red parent: \(R\)

Step 3: Progeny Genotypes and Phenotypes
- \(50\%\) of offspring are \(RR\) (Red flowered)
- \(50\%\) of offspring are \(Rr\) (Pink flowered)

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The expected progeny consists of red flowered as well as pink flowered plants.

answer.text: Red, Pink as well as white flowered plants
Red flowered as well as pink flowered plants

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q123 - Living tissues and xylem vessel characteristics

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I : Parenchyma is living but collenchyma is dead tissue.

Statement II : Gymnosperms lack xylem vessels but presence of xylem vessels is the characteristic of angiosperms.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Plant tissues are classified by living status and vascular cell composition.

Evaluation of Statements
- Statement I: Parenchyma is a living simple tissue. Collenchyma is also a living simple tissue with localized pectin wall thickenings at corners. Therefore, asserting that collenchyma is dead tissue is false.
- Statement II: Gymnosperms lack xylem vessels in their wood (except Gnetales), whereas the presence of xylem vessels is a defining anatomical feature of angiosperms (True).

Final Conclusion
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

answer.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q124 - Bt toxin specificity and gut pH activation

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I : Bt toxins are insect group specific and coded by a gene cry IAc.

Statement II : Bt toxin exists as inactive protoxin in B. thuringiensis. However, after ingestion by the insect the inactive protoxin gets converted into active form due to acidic pH of the insect gut.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Bacillus thuringiensis produces insecticidal crystal proteins (Bt toxins) encoded by cry genes.

Evaluation of Statements
- Statement I: Bt toxin proteins are insect group specific; for instance, cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms (True).
- Statement II: Bt toxin exists as an inactive crystalline protoxin in the bacterium. Upon ingestion by an insect, the protoxin is solubilized and converted into an active toxin due to the alkaline pH (not acidic pH) of the insect midgut. Therefore, claiming that activation occurs due to acidic pH is false.

Final Conclusion
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

answer.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q125 - Criteria for classification of kingdom fungi

questiontext.text: Which one of the following is not a criterion for classification of fungi?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The division of Kingdom Fungi into various classes (such as Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes, and Deuteromycetes) relies on specific morphological and reproductive characters.

Criteria Analysis
- The primary criteria used for classifying fungi into classes are:
1. Morphology of mycelium
2. Mode of spore formation
3. Type of fruiting bodies
- Mode of nutrition is heterotrophic (saprophytic or parasitic) across fungi and is not used as a criterion for dividing kingdom Fungi into its sub-classes.

Final Conclusion
Mode of nutrition is not a criterion for the classification of fungi.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q126 - Plant cell totipotency concept in tissue culture

questiontext.text: The capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell of the plant is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In plant tissue culture, cellular developmental potential allows complete plant regeneration under sterile nutrient conditions.

Definitions
- Totipotency: The inherent capacity of a single plant cell or explant to divide, differentiate, and regenerate into an entire plant.
- Differentiation: The structural and functional specialization of unspecialized cells.
- Somatic hybridization: Protoplast fusion between two different somatic cell lines.
- Micropropagation: The technique of producing large numbers of plants rapidly through tissue culture.

Final Conclusion
The capacity to generate a whole plant from any plant cell is called Totipotency.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q127 - Requirements for dark reaction of photosynthesis

questiontext.text:
Which of the following are required for the dark reaction of photosynthesis?

A. Light
B. Chlorophyll
C. CO2
D. ATP
E. NADPH

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Photosynthesis consists of light-dependent reactions (light reaction) and light-independent carbon-fixing reactions (dark reaction / Calvin cycle).

Requirements Analysis
- The light reaction occurs in thylakoid membranes, utilizing light and chlorophyll to generate \(\text{ATP}\), \(\text{NADPH}\), and \(\text{O}_2\).
- The dark reaction occurs in the stroma and does not directly require light or chlorophyll. Instead, it utilizes atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) (C) alongside the assimilatory power—\(\text{ATP}\) (D) and \(\text{NADPH}\) (E)—produced during light reactions to synthesize carbohydrates.

Final Conclusion
The components required for the dark reaction are \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{ATP}\), and \(\text{NADPH}\) (C, D and E only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q128 - Causes of high species richness in tropics

questiontext.text:
Tropical regions show greatest level of species richness because

A. Tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years, hence more time was available for species diversification.
B. Tropical environments are more seasonal.
C. More solar energy is available in tropics.
D. Constant environments promote niche specialization.
E. Tropical environments are constant and predictable.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Latitudinal gradients show that species diversity decreases from the equator towards the poles, with tropical regions harboring maximum biological diversity.

Hypotheses for High Tropical Diversity
1. Evolutionary time hypothesis: Tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed by glaciations for millions of years, allowing long evolutionary time for speciation (Statement A).
2. Environmental stability hypothesis: Tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively constant, and predictable (Statement E). Environment stability promotes niche specialization and greater species diversity (Statement D). Stating that tropics are more seasonal (Statement B) is false.
3. Solar energy hypothesis: Tropics receive more solar energy, contributing to higher primary productivity and indirectly supporting greater species richness (Statement C).

Final Conclusion
Statements A, C, D, and E account for the high species richness in tropical regions.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q129 - Identification of radicle in monocot seed

questiontext.text: Identify the part of the seed from the given figure which is destined to form root when the seed germinates.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Diagram Interpretation
The diagram depicts the longitudinal section (L.S.) of a monocotyledonous seed (maize grain).
Labels in the diagram:
- A points to coleoptile.
- B points to plumule.
- C points to radicle.
- D points to coleorhiza.

Step 2: Relevant Principles
In an embryonic axis, the plumule is destined to form the shoot system upon germination, whereas the radicle is destined to give rise to the primary root system.

Step 3: Evaluation
Label C points directly to the radicle at the basal region of the embryonic axis.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The seed structure destined to form the root system is represented by label C.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q130 - ATP and NADPH requirement per CO2 in Calvin cycle

questiontext.text: How many molecules of ATP and NADPH are required for every molecule of CO2 fixed in the Calvin cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Reaction Conditions
The Calvin cycle (C3 cycle) fixes atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) into 3-phosphoglycerate and subsequently regenerates Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (\(\text{RuBP}\)).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For fixing 1 molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\):
- Reduction stage: 2 molecules of \(\text{ATP}\) and 2 molecules of \(\text{NADPH}\) are consumed to convert 2 molecules of 3-PGA to 2 molecules of triose phosphate.
- Regeneration stage: 1 molecule of \(\text{ATP}\) is consumed to regenerate \(\text{RuBP}\) from triose phosphate.
Total energy cost per \(\text{CO}_2\) fixed = \(2 + 1 = 3\text{ ATP}\) and \(2\text{ NADPH}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Summing up energy inputs per single \(\text{CO}_2\) molecule fixed:
\[\text{ATP} = 2 \text{ (Reduction)} + 1 \text{ (Regeneration)} = 3\text{ ATP}\]
\[\text{NADPH} = 2 \text{ (Reduction)} = 2\text{ NADPH}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
For every molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixed, 3 molecules of ATP and 2 molecules of NADPH are required.

answer.text: 3 molecules of ATP and 3 molecules of NADPH
3 molecules of ATP and 2 molecules of NADPH
2 molecules of ATP and 3 molecules of NADPH
2 molecules of ATP and 2 molecules of NADPH

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q131 - Test cross genotype determination for dominant trait

questiontext.text: In a plant, black seed color (BB/Bb) is dominant over white seed color (bb). In order to find out the genotype of the black seed plant, with which of the following genotype will you cross it?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A test cross is used to determine whether an organism exhibiting a dominant phenotype is homozygous dominant or heterozygous.

Cross Design
- To perform a test cross, the individual with the dominant phenotype (\(BB\) or \(Bb\)) is crossed with an individual displaying the homozygous recessive phenotype (\(bb\)).
- If all progeny express the dominant phenotype, the tested plant is homozygous dominant (\(BB\)).
- If \(50\%\) of progeny express dominant and \(50\%\) express recessive phenotypes, the tested plant is heterozygous (\(Bb\)).

Final Conclusion
The black seed plant should be crossed with a plant of genotype \(bb\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q132 - Recognition sequence length of restriction enzyme Hind II

questiontext.text: Hind II always cuts DNA molecules at a particular point called recognition sequence and it consists of:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Restriction endonucleases inspect DNA length and cleave phosphodiester bonds at specific palindromic recognition sequences.

Enzymatic Characteristics
- Hind II was the first restriction endonuclease to be isolated.
- It specifically recognizes a 6 base pair palindromic DNA sequence (\(5'\text{-GTYRAC-}3'\), where Y is a pyrimidine and R is a purine) and cuts both strands between specific base pairs.

Final Conclusion
The recognition sequence of Hind II consists of 6 bp.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q133 - Function of bulliform cells in monocot leaves

questiontext.text: Bulliform cells are responsible for

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Bulliform or motor cells are specialized, large, empty, colorless epidermal cells located on the adaxial surface of leaves in grasses and monocots.

Physiological Role
- When bulliform cells absorb water and become turgid, the leaf surface is exposed and kept open.
- Under water stress or drought conditions, bulliform cells lose water, become flaccid, and cause the leaves to curl inwards to minimize transpiration surface area.

Final Conclusion
Bulliform cells are responsible for inward curling of leaves in monocots.

answer.text: Providing large spaces for storage of sugars.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q134 - Matching genetic terms with their definitions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II

List IList II
A. Two or more alternative forms of a geneI. Back cross
B. Cross of F1 progeny with homozygous recessive parentII. Ploidy
C. Cross of F1 progeny with any of the parentsIII. Allele
D. Number of chromosome sets in plantIV. Test cross

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Genetic terminology defines specific gene variants, breeding crosses, and chromosomal complements.

Matching Analysis
- Two or more alternative forms of a gene located at the same locus are called alleles (A matches III).
- A cross between an F1 progeny and its homozygous recessive parent is a test cross (B matches IV).
- A cross between an F1 progeny and either of its parents is a back cross (C matches I).
- The total number of complete chromosome sets in a plant cell defines its ploidy level (D matches II).

Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONA_Q135 - Selective action of synthetic auxin herbicide on lawns

questiontext.text: Auxin is used by gardeners to prepare weed-free lawns. But no damage is caused to grass as auxin

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) act as selective weedicides/herbicides.

Herbicide Selectivity
- 2,4-D is widely sprayed on lawns to eliminate broad-leaved dicotyledonous weeds.
- It does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants, permitting lawn grasses (monocots) to remain completely undamaged.

Final Conclusion
Auxin causes no damage to grass because it does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants.

answer.text: can help in cell division in grasses, to produce growth.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONB_Q137 - Molecular structure of chloroplast DNA

questiontext.text: The DNA present in chloroplast is:

Semi-autonomous organelle DNA shares evolutionary ancestry with prokaryotic genomes.

Organelle Genome Structure

- Like bacterial genomes and mitochondrial DNA, chloroplast DNA is double-stranded, naked (lacking histones), and circular.

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONB_Q138 - Description of wind pollinated corn cob inflorescence

name.text: NEET_UG_BOTANY_2024_SECTIONB_Q139 - Matching ecologists with their scientific contributions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II

List IList II
A. Robert MayI. Species-Area relationship
B. Alexander von HumboldtII. Long term ecosystem experiment using out door plots
C. Paul EhrlichIII. Global species diversity at about 7 million
D. David TilmanIV. Rivet popper hypothesis

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Ecological theories and quantitative estimates explain ecosystem diversity and stability.

Matching Analysis
- Robert May placed global species diversity at a conservative, scientifically sound estimate of about 7 million (A matches III).
- Alexander von Humboldt observed the species-area relationship during South American wilderness exploration, formulating \(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\) (B matches I).
- Paul Ehrlich proposed the Rivet Popper hypothesis to illustrate ecosystem degradation upon species loss (C matches IV).
